items.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: And he was a good friend of a flute player that I used to play with in Cleveland and who has since written a very well known book on jazz

ctx.x: When you got here you had to figure out how to put your knowledge into something that you could teach more than one-on-one too, in a classroom situation. That was sort of new ground at the time I would guess.

It really was, yeah. It took a fairly long period of six months to a year of really thinking back and asking myself well how did I learn to do this, and what records or what players did I listen to to develop this kind of technique or this way of playing and this approach to harmony, where did I learn this way of the rhythm section working together that was a little more conversational and not so style specific. So it was a really great learning experience for me. One of the people that was really helpful in…

history. It’s called Jazz Styles, it’s Mark Gridley. And when I knew I was going to have to put a jazz history course together there were so many deficiencies in my background of things that I didn’t know about, so I called Harvey, and he graciously gave up a lot of his time. I think I went over there for three or four Saturdays for four or five hours. And he had a huge record collection.
